hints: Think about what addition to a C=C double bond actually does, both new atoms add across the two carbons of the double bond.
With bromine, $Br_2$ adds to an alkene to give a dibromoalkane with the two Br atoms on neighbouring, adjacent carbons.
Look for the name where the two Br numbers are next to each other on a straight four carbon chain that matches $C_4H_8$ plus $Br_2$.
walkthrough:
**Recall addition to alkenes**

Remember, addition breaks the pi bond of C=C and attaches one new atom to each of the two double-bond carbons.

General rule for bromination:
$$C=C + Br_2 \rightarrow C(Br)-C(Br)$$

**Apply to a $C_4H_8$ alkene**

Take but-1-ene as an example, $CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2$. Adding $Br_2$ puts one Br on C1 and one Br on C2.

$$CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2 + Br_2 \rightarrow CH_3CH_2CHBrCH_2Br$$

**Name the product and choose**

The product $CH_3CH_2CHBrCH_2Br$ is a straight four carbon chain with Br on carbons 1 and 2. That is 1,2-dibromobutane, which must come from addition.

options.A: 1,1-dibromobutane has both Br atoms on the same carbon, $CH_3CH_2CH_2CBr_2H$. Addition across C=C always puts the two new atoms on two different, adjacent carbons, so a geminal 1,1 pattern cannot form this way.
options.B: 1,2-dibromobutane has Br atoms on adjacent carbons, $CH_3CH_2CHBrCH_2Br$. This is exactly what you get from electrophilic addition of $Br_2$ to but-1-ene, a $C_4H_8$ alkene.
options.C: 1,3-dibromobutane has Br atoms separated by one $CH_2$ group, $CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_2Br$. Addition puts both atoms across the original double bond, so they must end up next to each other, not with a gap.
options.D: 1,3-dibromomethylpropane implies a branched skeleton and Br atoms that are not on adjacent carbons. Addition to a $C_4H_8$ alkene preserves the carbon skeleton and gives vicinal Br atoms, so this cannot be an addition product.
